# Running a focus group

*It's really hard to design products by focus groups. A lot of times, people don't know what they want until you show it to them.* Steve Jobs as quoted in 

This chapter is based on a blog post I wrote in 2004 and slides from a course I have taught on Clinical Research Methodology.

A focus group is a meeting with multiple participants, either, where you ask questions and get responses from the participants. You can do this either live or via videoconferencing. There aren't too many differences. In a live focus group, you have an easier time identifying body language clues that might indicate trouble. Videoconferencing allows you to overcome travel constraints.

The recommendations for the number of participants in a focus group is six to ten. A few more or a few less is probably fine. You can't do a focus group with just one participant, though. A focus group with just one participant is more properly defined as an interview.

The group dynamics with multiple participants offers some advantages. First, it saves a bit of time compared to interviewing each participant separately. Second, the interaction of multiple participants may lead to a richer set of responses. One participant may elaborate on a point by another, either providing greater support or offering a countervailing opinion. Be careful, though, because participants may not raise certain issues in a group setting that they might talk about more openly in a one-on-one interview. You also have to worry about group dynamics, such as the steamroller who dominates the conversation or the wallflower who lets everyone else do all the talking.

## Step 1: Select a theoretical framework

If you are running a focus group, you have implicitly acknowledged your use of qualitative research. Good for you. Qualitative data is great stuff. It can put right at the doorstep of profound insights; insights that quantitative data can only wave at from a distance.

Once you are inside the qualitative data camp, your expectations are different. One thing you will have to face early is the theoretical framework that will guide your work. There are five general frameworks for qualitative research. You may decide to use a different framework or to not adopt any framework at all. Fine. Go ahead and travel to the beat of a different drum. Just recognize that those who might review your work will be looking for one these five approaches and will be disappointed when they don't see it.

The five theoretical frameworks are phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography, the case study, and narrative.

These approaches are all inductive (using specific findings to develop broader theories). You are trying to develop a framework of understanding. Don't go in with a heavy set of expectations. The research methodology is adaptive. How you collect information changes all along the way. This sounds subjective, but the qualitative data camp believes that you become more objective when you put aside your pre-conceived notions and assumptions and adapt your research approach during the study using the information that you get along the way.

Here is a brief description of the five frameworks.

**Phenomenology**. Phenomenology is the study of phenomenons. That's not a very helpful definition. Let me try again. A "phenomenon" is an event that you observe. Your goal in phenomenology is to find how different people place their own meaning on this event. 

**Grounded theory**. In grounded theory, you develop a new theory through the personal experiences of individuals. These experiences are primary: your theory is grounded in the data you collect and you need to put aside any existing theoretical beliefs. 

**Ethnography**. Derived originally from the fields of Sociology and Anthropology, ethnography has expanded into many different aspects of health care. It is the study of a group of people who share the same culture. Many resources on ethnography stressed the improtance of observation rather than interviewing, but this is still a valid framework for a focus group.

**Case study**. The case study is an in-depth examination of a case. It is not clear, to me anyway, what the difference is between a case and a phenomenon. The difference appears to be emphasis. In phenomenology, you want to understand perceptions about a phenomenon and wish to develop insights that can be generalized. In a case study, the emphasis is on understanding the particular case without any effort at generalization. The case is defined narrowly with respect to time, location, demographics, or other factors and tries to understand the unusual or the outlier rather than the typical or average.

The case study is not the same as a case report. The case report typically uses a factual reporting (mostly quantitative) of an unusual occurrence for a single patient.

**Narrative**. When I think of narrative, I think of the word "story." A narrative is a detailed account of an event placed in a structure and eveloped from a variety of perspectives. The structure could be chronology, stating with "once upon a time" and ending with "lived happily ever after". It might, however be organized by themes.

## Step 2: Set the stage

You have to have the right environment for a focus group. This can vary, but here are some common recommendations.

First, get two people. You can do this by yourself, but I don't recommend it. One person is the facilitator. Your roles as facilitator is is to guide the discussion. This means that you intervene if the group is getting off target or when you notice a steamroller or a wallflower. Doing this while still trying to keep neutral is not that easy. You should prepare some brief prompts to redirect the discussion or change the focus when needed.

The second person is the facilitator. If you are the facilitator, you don't say anything after the introductions. Instead, you run the recording device and take notes. The notes serve several purposes. First, they serve as a backup if your recording fails. Second, they note any significant non-verbal information such as gestures and body language. Third, the notes help to identify who is speaking when. A seating diagram is helpful for this. Note that not all focus groups track who is speaking.

After the session is complete, the two of you sit down in a debriefing session. Talk about how things went and how you might approach the next focus group. Next focus group? Yes. You did know that you couldn't get away with just one focus group. Part of the on-going analysis of focus group data is to examine the new themes that emerge with each successive focus group. 

## Step 3: Write and rewrite probe questions

Your should prepare a set of open-ended questions for the focus group including some follow-up prompts such as "Can you give a specific example of when this happened" or "What emotions did you feel at the time" or just simply "Tell me more about this." Don't be afraid to go off script if a new issue arises. You can comment on a facial expression with prompt like "You smiled/frowned at that last statement. Tell me brought that on."

Most importantly, use the results of one focus group to plan your next focus group. Revise your open-ended questions is they fall flat or if you need to investigate more deeply an issue that arose. This general strategy of letting the data influence the data collection process strikes some people as wrong. The qualitative camp, however, encourages this process.
